title: Serving a model: batch versus real time, cold starts, GPU versus CPU
story:
A model has to answer requests, and the hardware that runs it is expensive, slow to acquire and useless while idle. So the arrangement that gives the fastest single answer is rarely the one you can afford, and the decision is made by the shape of the demand rather than by the model.

Two shapes, with different economics. Predictable bulk work — scoring everything overnight, embedding a corpus, classifying a backlog — can be run as batches on saturated hardware, because nothing is waiting and utilisation can approach one. Unpredictable interactive work needs capacity held ready before the request arrives, because acquiring it afterwards takes longer than the request is willing to wait. The first pays for work; the second pays for readiness.

The cold start is the seam between them and it is worse than it sounds. The first request after a quiet period pays for acquiring hardware, loading weights and warming caches, and for a large model that is not a hundred milliseconds — it is long enough that the request times out. Which forces the choice: keep capacity warm and pay for idleness, or accept that some requests are catastrophically slow. There is no arrangement that avoids both, and pretending otherwise is how autoscaling policies get written that look sensible and fail in production.

What binds throughput once you are serving is memory rather than arithmetic, which the serving lesson established: high throughput requires batching many requests at a time, and the per-request cache is huge and grows and shrinks dynamically, being significantly wasted by fragmentation and redundant duplication when managed inefficiently, which limits the batch size. The classical waste is allocating a contiguous chunk sized to a request's maximum possible length, fragmenting severely when actual lengths are shorter and staying reserved for the request's lifetime.

Which leaves the question people skip, and the answer is more often than the industry suggests. Accelerators win when the work is large matrix arithmetic with enough parallelism to saturate them and enough batching to amortise the weights. Ordinary processors win when the model is small, the batch is one, the traffic is intermittent, or latency at low volume matters more than throughput — because an accelerator sitting idle between sporadic requests costs the same as one running flat out, and a small model on a processor you already have avoids the cold start entirely. Use the estimation figures: a datacenter round trip is around five hundred thousand nanoseconds, so moving work to a remote accelerator costs that before any arithmetic happens. If the model would run locally in less, the accelerator is a slower answer sold as a faster one.

problem.name: Serving shape
problem.shape: A model must answer requests on hardware that is expensive, slow to acquire, and costs the same whether busy or idle.
tell: utilisation is low and the bill is not
the first request after a quiet period times out
an accelerator is being used for a small model at batch size one
latency targets and cost targets are being pursued with the same configuration
problem.move: Classify the demand before choosing hardware. Run predictable bulk work as batches at high utilisation, hold capacity ready only for the interactive work that needs it, and check whether the model is small enough that ordinary processors beat a remote accelerator once the round trip is counted.
problem.invariant: Batching amortises the cost of moving the weights across every request in the batch, so throughput per unit cost rises with batch size — and batch size is bounded by per-request memory rather than by arithmetic.
problem.breaks: Cold start makes the two economics irreconcilable. Capacity held ready is paid for while idle, and capacity acquired on demand arrives after the request that needed it — so there is no configuration that is both cheap at low traffic and fast on the first request, only a choice about which failure you prefer.

cost.time: queueing while a batch forms for throughput, or idle capacity held for latency; never neither
cost.space: per-request cache proportional to how much has been generated, which is what actually caps concurrency
cost.beats: one replica per request, which leaves the arithmetic idle, and worst-case memory reservation, which holds expensive memory that is mostly empty

worked.problem: When is it correct to serve a model on ordinary processors rather than accelerators?
worked.reasoning:
More often than the default assumption suggests, and the deciding factors are batch size, model size, traffic shape and whether the accelerator is remote.

Start with what an accelerator is for. It wins on large matrix arithmetic with enough parallelism to saturate it, and it wins more the larger the batch, because the dominant cost is moving the weights and batching amortises that across everyone in the batch. Both conditions matter. An accelerator running a small model at batch size one is doing very little of what it is good at while costing what it costs.

So the cases where ordinary processors win. Small models, where the arithmetic fits comfortably and the parallelism is not there to exploit. Batch size one, which is the common case for genuinely interactive single-user work and which removes the amortisation argument entirely. Intermittent traffic, because an accelerator idle between sporadic requests costs the same as one running flat out, and utilisation is the whole economic case. And latency at low volume, where you care about one answer quickly rather than many answers cheaply.

The argument people miss is the round trip. A datacenter round trip is around five hundred thousand nanoseconds — half a millisecond — before any arithmetic happens. If the model would run locally in less time than that, sending it to a remote accelerator is a slower answer being sold as a faster one. That calculation is worth doing explicitly, because the instinct that accelerators are faster is about arithmetic throughput and the question is about end-to-end latency.

There is also the cold start, which pushes in the same direction. The first request after a quiet period pays for acquiring hardware, loading weights and warming caches, and for a large model that is long enough to exceed a request timeout. A small model on processors you already have avoids that entirely, which is worth a great deal on traffic that is bursty.

What would move me back toward accelerators: a model large enough that processors cannot hold it or run it at acceptable speed, traffic steady enough to keep the hardware busy, and batching sufficient to amortise the weight movement. Those three together are the case, and they are usually present in high-volume production serving and usually absent in the internal tool somebody is about to over-provision.

And the honest summary I would give: the question is not which hardware is faster. It is what fraction of the time the expensive hardware will be doing the thing it is expensive for.

problem.practice: Take a model you serve on an accelerator and measure how long it takes on ordinary processors at batch size one. Then add your datacenter round trip to the accelerator path. Compare the totals, and separately compute what fraction of the last week that accelerator was actually busy.

beats.broke: A model has to answer requests, and the hardware that runs it is expensive, slow to acquire and useless while idle — so the arrangement giving the fastest single answer is rarely the one you can afford.
beats.fix: Decide by the shape of the demand rather than by the model: predictable bulk work runs as batches on saturated hardware, unpredictable interactive work needs capacity held ready, and the two have different economics.
beats.cost: Holding capacity ready is paying for idleness, and not holding it means the first request after a quiet period pays for loading everything — there is no arrangement that avoids both.

interview.q: When is it correct to serve a model on ordinary processors rather than accelerators?
interview.trap: Assuming accelerators are always faster. That instinct is about arithmetic throughput — at batch size one, on a small model, with a datacenter round trip in front of it, the accelerator can be the slower end-to-end answer while costing the same whether busy or idle.
